The **C9 League** (九校联盟) is an inter-university seminar composed of nine public universities in China. It was established on May 4, 1998 at the 100th anniversary of Peking University. 




## Membership

[edit]

The C9 league comprises nine public universities:[1]




</fragment>
<fragment>
* Fudan University – Shanghai
* Shanghai Jiao Tong University – Shanghai
* Harbin Institute of Technology – Harbin, Heilongjiang
* Nanjing University – Nanjing, Jiangsu
* Peking University – Beijing
* Tsinghua University – Beijing
* University of Science and Technology of China – Hefei, Anhui
* Xi'an Jiaotong University – Xi'an, Shaanxi
* Zhejiang University – Hangzhou, Zhejiang


All C9 League schools are part of the former Project 985, Project 211, Plan 111, as well as the current Double First Class University Plan.[2][3] In 2014, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences started to participate in the C9 League meetings.[4]

<document>
<title>Fudan University</title>
<fragment>

Fudan is a member of the C9 League, Project 985, Project 211, and the Double First Class University identified by the Ministry of Education of China. It is also a member of Universitas 21, Washington University's McDonnell International Scholars Academy, and the Association of Pacific Rim Universities, BRICS Universities League, Association of East Asian Research Universities, and Council on Business & Society.


Fudan University is a member of the Consortium of Academic Stewards for The Scholar Ship. The university is also a member of China Center Austria and partner of the Austrian Business School SMBS.


In February 2008, Fudan University launched the Fudan University Education Development Foundation in New York. [40]


In 1995, Fudan established the Nordic Centre in Shanghai, a joint platform for research and education with 14 universities from Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden. By 2012, the Nordic Centre Fudan has 27 member institutions in 5 Nordic countries.[41]


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Fudan lost its "National" appellation and became Fudan University to reflect the fact that all universities under the new socialist state would be public. Fudan was the first university to be reorganized by the new government in 1952 and modeled on Soviet education. The original departments were changed, with arts and sciences departments from at least ten other universities in eastern China being added.[*citation needed*] Parts of Aurora University merged into Fudan in 1952.


In the late 1970s, after the Cultural Revolution, the university was converted to a modern, comprehensive[*clarification needed*] university.[*citation needed*]


Fudan University and Shanghai Medical University merged in 2000.[5]

**Fudan University** (复旦大学) is a national public university in Shanghai, China. The university is affiliated with the Ministry of Education, and is co-sponsored by the ministry and Shanghai City. The university is part of Project 985, Project 211, and the Double First Class University Plan.


Fudan has five undergraduate colleges – Zhide (志德), Tengfei (腾飞), Keqing (克卿), Renzhong (任重), and Xide (希德). The university has four campuses in Shanghai – Handan (邯郸), Fenglin (枫林), Zhangjiang (张江), and Jiangwan (江湾) – which share the same central administration. It also has 17 affiliated hospitals. The university is a member of the C9 League.

<document>
<title>History of Tsinghua University</title>
<fragment>
Tsinghua received a charter from the Republic of China (ROC) in 1928 and became a national university. At the onset of Second Sino-Japanese War, Tsinghua, Peking University and Nankai University moved to Changsha and formed the National Changsha Provisional University. The combined school relocated to Kunming in 1938 and was renamed as National Southwest Associated University.


Tsinghua was restored in 1946 at Tsinghua Garden. It became one of the National Key Universities of the People's Republic of China following education policy reforms starting in 1952. The National Tsing Hua University at Hsinchu, Taiwan was formed in 1956 by Tsinghua academics who fled the communist revolution.



## Early PRC

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
History of Tsinghua University

![](image)Qinghua Xuetang, the old building of the former Tsinghua College.
Founded in 1911, the Tsinghua University is located on the site of Tsinghua Garden in Beijing, the former residence of Prince Yinzhi, the third son of the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty.


In 1909, the indemnity payment to the United States from the Boxer Protocol was reduced by US$10.8 million by Theodore Roosevelt's administration. The Qing imperial court used the difference to create the Boxer Indemnity Scholarship Programme and established the China Institute along with a preparatory school. The school was later renamed *Tsinghua School* and expanded in 1925 with the addition of a college department.




## Origins

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Between 1970 and 1975, Tsinghua University made large-scale changes to its organization. In 1970, the school planned to put in place three factories, the experimental chemistry factory, automotive factory, and the precise instrument and machine tool factory. The school now had seven majors: electrical engineering, industrial automation, chemical engineering, infrastructure engineering, hydraulic works engineering, engineering physics, and engineering mechanics mathematics. There was a mechanical repair military company and also basic university courses. The school had two "branch campuses": the Mianyang campus and the Jiangxi campus (the model farm at Nanchang). In 1972, a rural campus was established in Daxing and a hydraulics works facility was established in Sanmenxia. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)The first batch of Chinese students to study in the United States in 1909
The United States government begin to remit the difference in 1909. In May, Tenney Charles Daniel was assigned to represent the United States government in the study programme. The selection of students was finalised after a series of discussion in June, and the proposal received the imperial approval on 10 July. The office for the study programme was officially set up on 17 July.[Note 1] On 25 August, Zhou Ziqi[Note 2] and Tang Guo'an were appointed to the board of directors to run the office operations.[7] Tsinghua Garden was transferred to the study programme office to establish the preparatory school.[8]



![](image)The inscription on the plaque of Tsinghua Garden written by the Xianfeng Emperor.
## Republican era

Based on the Wikipedia article content I was able to access, I can provide you with comprehensive information about the founding and early history of Peking University:

## Founding Year
**1898** - The Imperial University of Peking was formally established on July 3, 1898.

## Key Context about the Founding

**Political Context**: The university was founded during the **Hundred Days' Reform** period (戊戌变法), a period of rapid political and social reform in late Qing Dynasty China.

**Founding Process**: 
- Following China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War, intellectuals including **Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao, and Yan Fu** called for educational reforms
- In June 1896, **Minister Li Duanfen** proposed creating a university in the capital
- On **June 11, 1898**, the **Guangxu Emperor** authorized the creation of what became the **Imperial University of Peking** (京师大学堂)
- The university was formally established on **July 3, 1898** when the emperor approved the royal charter written by **Liang Qichao**
- **Minister Sun Jianai** was charged with the implementation

<document>
<title>Fudan University</title>
<fragment>

In 1917, Fudan Public School became a private university named the Private Fudan University, and also had a middle school and university-preparatory school. In 1929, Fudan reorganized its departments, expanding to include departments of journalism, municipals[*clarification needed*], law, and education.[4]


After the Japanese invasion of China in 1937, Fudan moved with the Kuomintang government to the inland city of Chongqing, the wartime Chinese capital. On December 25, 1941, the First Meeting of Fifth Conference of the Highest Executive Authority of the National Government of the Republic of China voted to change Fudan University (Chongqing) to a public university with Wu Nanxuan as its president. Fudan University then became National Fudan University. After the end of World War II, it moved back to Shanghai.[*citation needed*]



### 1949 - present

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Fudan lost its "National" appellation and became Fudan University to reflect the fact that all universities under the new socialist state would be public. Fudan was the first university to be reorganized by the new government in 1952 and modeled on Soviet education. The original departments were changed, with arts and sciences departments from at least ten other universities in eastern China being added.[*citation needed*] Parts of Aurora University merged into Fudan in 1952.


In the late 1970s, after the Cultural Revolution, the university was converted to a modern, comprehensive[*clarification needed*] university.[*citation needed*]


Fudan University and Shanghai Medical University merged in 2000.[5]

Fudan University, then romanized as **Fuh Tan**, was founded as Fudan Public School in 1905, by Ma Xiangbo, SJ, who had resigned from Aurora University. The two Chinese characters *Fu* (復, means "again") and *Dan* (旦, means "morning", "light" ), meaning both "(heavenly light shines) day after day" and "Aurora Revived", were chosen by Ma on the recommendation of Yu You-jen, from the Confucian Classic *Shangshu Dazhuan* (Chinese: 尙書大傳): "Itinerant as the twilight, sun glows and moon luminesces" (Chinese: 日月光華，旦復旦兮). The university motto "Scientia et studium, quaestio et cogitatio" comes from Analects Book 19.6 (Chinese: 博學而篤志，切問而近思), which means "rich in knowledge and tenacious of purposes, inquiring with earnestness and reflecting with self-practice".

**Nanjing University** (**NJU**; Chinese: 南京大学) is a national public university in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. It is affiliated and sponsored by the Ministry of Education. The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.


Established in 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School, Nanjing University underwent a number of name changes, such as Nanjing Higher Normal School, National Southeastern University and National Central University, until it was renamed Nanjing University in 1950. It merged with the University of Nanking in 1952.[6]


Nanjing University has two main campuses: the Xianlin campus in the northeast of Nanjing, and the Gulou campus in the city center of Nanjing. The university is a member of the C9 League.




## History

[edit]




</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** According to The History Evolution of National Central University (R.O.C. 26, 1937 CE) (《國立中央大學沿革史》 中華民國二十六年), it was founded in the winter of the first year of Yong'an reign (258 CE) during the era of Three Kingdoms. Since it was founded in CE 258, it had evolved and adopted different names in each dynasty or period in ancient China. It became a modern institution of higher learning in 1902 during Qing dynasty. Liangjiang Higher Normal School was closed in 1911 when the Qing dynasty was overthrown. In 1915 after the Republic of China was founded, Nanking Higher Normal School was established to replace the Liangjing Normal School. In 1949 when the Republic of China was replaced by the People's Republic of China in mainland, its name was changed from National Central University (国立中央大学) to Nanjing University (南京大学).

</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Old Great Hall (大禮堂)
More than 1500 years ago, ancient University of Nanjing founded the earliest faculties of literature, history, etc.. In modern times, Nanjing University established Chinese first faculties of art, gymnastics, biology, psychology, business management, etc.. Its faculties, departments and schools have been changed and evolved timely. For example, in 1921, the university consisted of 5 schools: liberal arts, education, agriculture, engineering and business, in 1928 the school of liberal arts had become three schools, and the university consisted of 8 schools: humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, education, agriculture, engineering, business and medicine, and now, many former departments of humanities, natural sciences and social sciences have become schools.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In 1952, many colleges and departments, mainly colleges of education (or teacher, normal, including art and physical education departments), engineering, agriculture, and medicine, were split from Nanjing University, and many new independent schools were formed, including Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing Institute of Technology which was located at former Nanjing University site and later renamed Southeast University, etc.[Note 5] At the same time, University of Nanking, a private university established in 1888 and sponsored by American churches, was merged into Nanjing University (南京大學), which lost its "national" appellation in 1950 to reflect the reality that all universities in the PRC would be public, and Nanjing University moved campus to the site of University of Nanking where was west to Gulou Mountain and was also once the site of imperial Nanjing University in ancient times. A separate National Central University was reinstated in Taiwan by its old alumni association in 1962.




</fragment>

<document>
<title>Zhang Zhidong</title>
<fragment>

Kang Youwei, another late Qing reformist, later expressed similar mode of thinking - he also advocated aiding modern education at the cost of temples. However, Kang Youwei is more radical as he envisions destruction of religions in comparison to Zhang's conservative approach. ## 1. Sanjiang Normal School Founding in 1902

**Founders:** Zhang Zhidong, Liu Kunyi, and Wei Guangtao were the founders of Sanjiang Normal College.

**Original Purpose:** The institution was established to modernize education in China, drawing inspiration from the Japanese educational system. Zhang Zhidong specifically announced plans to hire 12 Japanese teachers before establishing the college.

- In 1910, it merged with The Union Christian College and became the Private University of Nanking (金陵大學)
- In 1951, Ginling Women's College merged into University of Nanking
- **In 1952, University of Nanking was merged with Nanjing University**

- **1915:** Nanjing Higher Normal School was established to replace the Liangjiang Normal School after the Republic of China was founded

## 1. Founding Year and Origins

**Primary Founding:** 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School

**Ancient Legacy:** Nanjing University claims intellectual lineage dating back to 258 CE during the Three Kingdoms period, but it became a modern institution of higher learning in 1902 during the Qing dynasty.

## 2. Founders and Original Purpose

**Founders:** Zhang Zhidong, Liu Kunyi, and Wei Guangtao

**Original Purpose:** The institution was established to modernize education in China, drawing inspiration from the Japanese educational system. Zhang Zhidong specifically announced plans to hire 12 Japanese teachers before establishing the college, demonstrating the international approach to China's educational modernization.

**Historical Context:** Zhang Zhidong succeeded Liu Kunyi as Viceroy of Liangjiang in 1901 and moved to Nanjing, where he laid the foundations for what would become Nanjing University. Liu Kunyi died in 1902, shortly after submitting joint memorials on reform to the Emperor.

## 3. Early Name Changes and Reorganizations

The institutional evolution was complex, with several key transitions:

**Chronology of Name Changes:**
- **1902:** Sanjiang Normal School (founding)
- **1911:** Liangjiang Higher Normal School (closed when Qing dynasty was overthrown)
- **1915:** Nanjing Higher Normal School (established after Republic of China founding to replace Liangjiang)
- Later: National Southeastern University
- Later: National Central University
- **1949:** Renamed Nanjing University when PRC replaced ROC in mainland China
- **1950:** Lost "national" appellation to reflect that all PRC universities would be public

## 4. Major 1952 Merger

In 1952, a significant reorganization occurred:
- The University of Nanking (founded 1888 by C.H. Fowler, originally the first educational institution in China officially named "university" in English) was merged into Nanjing University
- Many colleges and departments were split from Nanjing University to form new independent schools, including Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing Institute of Technology (later Southeast University), etc.
- This merger shifted Nanjing University's campus location to the site of the former University of Nanking

## Key Historical Highlights

- The university went through a complete closure during the 1911-1915 period due to the fall of the Qing dynasty
- The 1952 reorganization was part of broader Chinese educational restructuring
- The institution has a claimed 1,700+ year intellectual lineage but only became a modern comprehensive university in 1902

This complex founding history reflects the turbulent political changes in China during the early 20th century, with the university evolving through several distinct institutional phases while maintaining academic continuity.

<title>National Chiao Tung University</title>
<fragment>

NCTU was merged with National Yang-Ming University into the newly formed **National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University** on 1 February 2021.[8]




## History

[edit]

### Qing dynasty

[edit]

National Chiao Tung University was founded in Xujiahui, the suburbs of Shanghai in 1896, sixteen years before the birth of the Republic of China, at the suggestion of Sheng Xuanhuai, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Qing dynasty. The university was first named Nanyang College. It was established to meet the need to introduce western civilization into China. The college focused only on politics, law, and translations of western books. In the later years of the Qing dynasty, the college was renamed the Vocational College of Higher Education and was governed by the Ministry of Post and Transportation. By including new vocational programs, such as business, electrical engineering, shipping management, and railway management, the college played a major role in science and engineering education in modern China.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1926 the Shanghai campus established its Institute of Industry, which was devoted to telecommunication research. At the end of the Northern Expedition in 1928, the university resumed the name of Chiao Tung University and was governed by the newly established Ministry of Railways of the nationalist government. The Shanghai campus thereafter developed into four Colleges: the Colleges of Railway Management, the Colleges of Civil Engineering, the Colleges of Mechanical Engineering, and the Colleges of Electrical Engineering. In 1930, the College of Science consisting of three departments: Mathematics, Science, and Chemistry, was added to the campus. At the same time, the Institute of Industry in Shanghai was expanded to include the Institute of Industry and the Institute of Economics.


</fragment>

**National Chiao Tung University** (**NCTU**; Chinese: 國立交通大學) was a public research university located in Hsinchu, Taiwan. Established in 1896 as Nanyang Public School by an imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, it was one of China's leading universities. After the Chinese Civil War, NCTU was re-established by former Chiao Tung University faculty and alumni in Taiwan in 1958.


NCTU was selected by Taiwan's Ministry of Educations as one of the seven national universities focused on research in 2002.[4][5] It was subsequently chosen to pursue all-around excellence with "versatile international competitiveness to continuously strengthen international academic influence and visibility".[6][7]


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, the four campuses of the college were reorganized and governed by the Ministry of Transportation, which evolved from the original Qing dynasty Ministry of Post and Transportation. The names of the Vocational College of Higher Education, the Railway College, and the Railway Management College were changed respectively to the Shanghai Industrial College, the Tang-Shan Industrial College, and the College of Management in Railway, Post and Telecommunications. In 1921, the Ministry of Transportation united these three campuses under a single name: Chiao Tung University. The university reorganized its administrative systems, enlarged its facilities, and formed a new board of trustees. Later on, these three campuses were separated and reunited several times and their names were changed repeatedly because of political turmoil.


</fragment>

In 1896, the **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學) was founded in Shanghai by the imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, under the Business and Telegraphs Office of the Qing imperial government. Four schools were established: a normal school, a school of foreign studies, a middle school, and a high school. Sheng Xuanhuai, the mandarin who proposed the idea to the Guangxu Emperor, became the first president and is, along with missionary educator John Calvin Ferguson, regarded as the university's founder.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The university was established on April 8, 1896 as **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學; *Nányáng Gōngxué*) by an imperial edict.[6][7] The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.[8] The university underwent a number of reformations and gained its current name in 1959. Shanghai Second Medical University was merged into the university on July 18, 2005.[9] It is a member of the C9 League.




## Name

[edit]

The word *Jiāotōng* (交通) (historically, **Chiao-t'ung**) means "transportation" or "communication". It reflects the university's roots — it was founded by the Ministry of Posts and Communications of the late Qing dynasty.[*citation needed*] Engineering and managerial sciences are major academic focuses at the various Jiaotong universities, but not the only fields of research.

<title>National Chiao Tung University</title>
<fragment>

NCTU was merged with National Yang-Ming University into the newly formed **National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University** on 1 February 2021.[8]




## History

[edit]

### Qing dynasty

[edit]

National Chiao Tung University was founded in Xujiahui, the suburbs of Shanghai in 1896, sixteen years before the birth of the Republic of China, at the suggestion of Sheng Xuanhuai, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Qing dynasty. The university was first named Nanyang College. It was established to meet the need to introduce western civilization into China. The college focused only on politics, law, and translations of western books. In the later years of the Qing dynasty, the college was renamed the Vocational College of Higher Education and was governed by the Ministry of Post and Transportation. By including new vocational programs, such as business, electrical engineering, shipping management, and railway management, the college played a major role in science and engineering education in modern China.


</fragment>

**National Chiao Tung University** (**NCTU**; Chinese: 國立交通大學) was a public research university located in Hsinchu, Taiwan. Established in 1896 as Nanyang Public School by an imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, it was one of China's leading universities. After the Chinese Civil War, NCTU was re-established by former Chiao Tung University faculty and alumni in Taiwan in 1958.


NCTU was selected by Taiwan's Ministry of Educations as one of the seven national universities focused on research in 2002.[4][5] It was subsequently chosen to pursue all-around excellence with "versatile international competitiveness to continuously strengthen international academic influence and visibility".[6][7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1926 the Shanghai campus established its Institute of Industry, which was devoted to telecommunication research. At the end of the Northern Expedition in 1928, the university resumed the name of Chiao Tung University and was governed by the newly established Ministry of Railways of the nationalist government. The Shanghai campus thereafter developed into four Colleges: the Colleges of Railway Management, the Colleges of Civil Engineering, the Colleges of Mechanical Engineering, and the Colleges of Electrical Engineering. In 1930, the College of Science consisting of three departments: Mathematics, Science, and Chemistry, was added to the campus. At the same time, the Institute of Industry in Shanghai was expanded to include the Institute of Industry and the Institute of Economics.


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, the four campuses of the college were reorganized and governed by the Ministry of Transportation, which evolved from the original Qing dynasty Ministry of Post and Transportation. The names of the Vocational College of Higher Education, the Railway College, and the Railway Management College were changed respectively to the Shanghai Industrial College, the Tang-Shan Industrial College, and the College of Management in Railway, Post and Telecommunications. In 1921, the Ministry of Transportation united these three campuses under a single name: Chiao Tung University. The university reorganized its administrative systems, enlarged its facilities, and formed a new board of trustees. Later on, these three campuses were separated and reunited several times and their names were changed repeatedly because of political turmoil.


</fragment>

In 1896, the **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學) was founded in Shanghai by the imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, under the Business and Telegraphs Office of the Qing imperial government. Four schools were established: a normal school, a school of foreign studies, a middle school, and a high school. Sheng Xuanhuai, the mandarin who proposed the idea to the Guangxu Emperor, became the first president and is, along with missionary educator John Calvin Ferguson, regarded as the university's founder.

The university was established on April 8, 1896 as **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學; *Nányáng Gōngxué*) by an imperial edict.[6][7] The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.[8] The university underwent a number of reformations and gained its current name in 1959. Shanghai Second Medical University was merged into the university on July 18, 2005.[9] It is a member of the C9 League.




## Name

[edit]

The word *Jiāotōng* (交通) (historically, **Chiao-t'ung**) means "transportation" or "communication". It reflects the university's roots — it was founded by the Ministry of Posts and Communications of the late Qing dynasty.[*citation needed*] Engineering and managerial sciences are major academic focuses at the various Jiaotong universities, but not the only fields of research.

Taking active part in the Self-Strengthening Movement, He actively advocated using Western technology in saving the country from destitution. In 1896, he also founded the forerunner of Jiaotong University, which was later divided into Shanghai Jiaotong University and Xi'an Jiaotong University. In 1896, the **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學) was founded in Shanghai by the imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, under the Business and Telegraphs Office of the Qing imperial government. Four schools were established: a normal school, a school of foreign studies, a middle school, and a high school. Sheng Xuanhuai, the mandarin who proposed the idea to the Guangxu Emperor, became the first president and is, along with missionary educator John Calvin Ferguson, regarded as the university's founder.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The university was established on April 8, 1896 as **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學; *Nányáng Gōngxué*) by an imperial edict.[6][7] The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.[8] The university underwent a number of reformations and gained its current name in 1959. Shanghai Second Medical University was merged into the university on July 18, 2005.[9] It is a member of the C9 League.




## Name

[edit]

The word *Jiāotōng* (交通) (historically, **Chiao-t'ung**) means "transportation" or "communication". It reflects the university's roots — it was founded by the Ministry of Posts and Communications of the late Qing dynasty.[*citation needed*] Engineering and managerial sciences are major academic focuses at the various Jiaotong universities, but not the only fields of research.



## History

<title>Sheng Xuanhuai</title>
<fragment>
![](image)Sheng Xuanhuai's calligraphy
Taking active part in the Self-Strengthening Movement, He actively advocated using Western technology in saving the country from destitution. His influence was mainly felt in the southern part of China, specifically in Shanghai. By 1893, Sheng controlled China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company, established the Imperial Telegraphy Administration and created first successful cotton mill in China. In 1896, he took over the Hanyang ironworks and related mines, along with control of the newly created imperial railway administration.[1]


In 1895, he founded Beiyang University, the first institution of modern higher education in China. In 1896, he also founded the forerunner of Jiaotong University, which was later divided into Shanghai Jiaotong University and Xi'an Jiaotong University. He also created eleven "first", including the first modern bank, first telegraphy company, the first iron and steel joint enterprise....[2]

After the Boxer Uprising, in 1900 when Eight Nation Alliance entered Peking, Sheng and Ronglu initiated the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, resisting Empress Dowager Cixi's Imperial Decree of declaration of war against foreign powers. <title>John Calvin Ferguson</title>
<fragment>

In 1889, Ferguson used the living room of his house in Nanjing for classes; these grew into Huiwen Shuyuan, which in turn evolved into the University of Nanking. In 1897 he was offered a position by Sheng Xuanhuai, a pioneering industrialist and well-connected entrepreneur whom he had met by chance a few years earlier when they were both on a Yangtze river boat. Sheng was impressed by Ferguson's learned Chinese and courtly manner and invited him to found a second western-style school, the Nanyang Public School, Shanghai, a predecessor of the Jiaotong (Transportation) University, which later split into three independent institutions: National Chiao Tung University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Xi'an Jiaotong University.[2] In 1897, to facilitate faculty and students getting to and from the school, he built a road in the Shanghai French Concession with his own salary,[3] which was later named Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road).[4]

When Ferguson resigned as president of the Nanyang school, with Sheng Xuanhuai's continuing sponsorship, he became foreign secretary to the Chinese Ministry of Commerce in 1903, and then was official or informal advisor to government bureaus and the chief secretary of the Imperial Chinese Railway Administration until 1907. Taking advantage of his knowledge and connections he began to acquire Chinese art for the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, Ferguson was a member of the committee to catalog the imperial palace collections of art.[1]

These volumes were unsystematic in the works they had access to and haphazard in their organization, but they made it possible to know the range and nature of Chinese art at a time when most of the important pieces were emerging from imperial or private collections which had not been available to the public or scholars.[2]


Ferguson donated many pieces to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, but the bulk of his own collection, including bronzes, scrolls, paintings, and jades, was donated to Nanjing University in 1935, and other major gifts were made which are now in the collections of Shanghai Jiao Tong University.[1]

<title>Tianjin University</title>
<fragment>
In 1895, Sheng Xuanhuai submitted his memorial to the Guangxu Emperor to request for approval to set up a modern higher education institution in Tianjin. After approval on October 2, 1895, **Peiyang Western Study College** was founded by him and American educator Charles Daniel Tenney and later developed to Peiyang University. It was the first university providing four year degree modern higher education in China.[8] The university modeled itself on the famous American Universities and aimed to rejuvenate China by training qualified personnel with new scientific and technological knowledge. After the PR China's foundation and university restructures, Peiyang University was renamed Tianjin University in 1951.[9]




</fragment>
<fragment>

**Tianjin University** (**TJU**; 天津大学), previously **Peiyang University** (北洋大學), is a national public research university in Tianjin, China. Established in 1895 by a royal charter from Guangxu Emperor, Tianjin University is the oldest university in China, leading the country's significant shift towards modernization and development.[3][4][5] The university is affiliated with and sponsored by the Ministry of Education of China. It is a member of the national Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.[6]

## Background: Sheng Xuanhuai's Vision

Sheng Xuanhuai (1844-1916) was a pioneering Chinese industrialist and statesman during the Self-Strengthening Movement. According to historical records, he **founded multiple educational institutions**:

- **1895**: Established Beiyang University (now Tianjin University) - the first modern university in China with four-year degree programs
- **1896**: Founded the forerunner institution that became Nanyang Public School, which later evolved into Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Xi'an Jiaotong University

## Educational Structure and Management

### Management Model
Nanyang Public School was established with a **Western educational model** as part of Sheng Xuanhuai's broader vision for modernizing China through practical education. The management structure included:

1. **International Leadership**: In 1897, Sheng hired **John Calvin Ferguson**, an American educator, to found and lead Nanyang Public School. Ferguson was chosen specifically for his knowledge of both Chinese and Western educational systems.

2. **Sponsorship and Oversight**: Sheng Xuanhuai provided continuing sponsorship and maintained oversight as the school developed.

### Educational Direction and Curriculum

The school's educational philosophy aligned with the broader **"Self-Strengthening Movement"** approach, which was summarized as **"Chinese Learning as Substance, Western Learning for Application"** (中学为体，西学为用).

However, Nanyang Public School specifically focused on:

1. **Technical and Professional Education**: Given its connection to the imperative of modernizing China, the school emphasized:
   - Engineering and technology
   - Transportation (reflected in its later evolution into Jiaotong/Transportation University)
   - Practical sciences and Western technical knowledge

2. **Limited Traditional Elements**: Unlike some institutions that tried to balance traditional Confucian education with Western learning, Nanyang Public School appears to have been more focused on practical, modern education from its inception.

## Analysis of Your Specific Concerns

### 1. Normal School Education (师范教育)
Based on the available historical information, **Nanyang Public School was not primarily established as a normal school** (teacher training institution). Its focus was on:
- Technical and engineering education
- Transportation and industrial technology
- Preparing students for modern administrative and industrial roles

This oriented approach was typical of the Self-Strengthening Movement's emphasis on practical knowledge over traditional scholarly pursuits.

### 2. Traditional Arts and Cultural Education
There is **no evidence from available sources** that traditional Chinese arts and cultural education were major components of Nanyang Public School's curriculum during 1896-1911. The institution appears to have been:
- More practically oriented
- Focused on Western scientific and technical knowledge
- Designed to serve China's industrial and administrative modernization needs

### 3. The "Hypocrisy" Culture
Your observation about potential hypocrisy between learning Western knowledge while preaching traditional Chinese values is historically astute. However, Nanyang Public School's approach seems to have been **more straightforward** than many institutions of that era:

- **Clear Mission**: The school's mission appears to have been openly focused on practical, Western-style education for China's modernization, rather than attempting to maintain a facade of traditional values while embracing Western models.

- **Transparency in Approach**: Unlike some institutions that tried to present a Confucian face while secretly pursuing Westernization, Nanyang Public School's mission was apparently more transparent about its modernizing objectives.

## Historical Context and Legacy

The period 1896-1911 represented a crucial transition in Chinese education:
- **1905**: Abolition of the traditional civil service examination system (part of the Late Qing reforms)
- Shift from **traditional Confucian education** to **modern scientific and technical education**
- Recognition that China's survival depended on mastery of Western technology and administrative methods

## Conclusion

Nanyang Public School under Sheng Xuanhuai's direction appears to have been:

1. **Strongly practical and technically oriented**, focusing on engineering, transportation, and modern administration
2. **Managed with Western expertise** (John Calvin Ferguson's leadership)
3. **Relatively free** from the extensive normal school or traditional arts components that characterized some other educational experiments of the era
4. **Less hypocritical** than some contemporaries in its clear commitment to Western-style practical education for China's modernization

The institution's evolution into today's prestigious Shanghai Jiao Tong University system reflects this original focus on practical, technical education rather than traditional scholarly or arts education.

**Sources**: Historical records from Wikipedia entries on Sheng Xuanhuai, John Calvin Ferguson, Tianjin University, Self-Strengthening Movement, and Late Qing reforms provide this comprehensive picture of Nanyang Public School's educational philosophy and management during this critical period in Chinese educational history.

In 1896, the **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學) was founded in Shanghai by the imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, under the Business and Telegraphs Office of the Qing imperial government. Four schools were established: a normal school, a school of foreign studies, a middle school, and a high school. Sheng Xuanhuai, the mandarin who proposed the idea to the Guangxu Emperor, became the first president and is, along with missionary educator John Calvin Ferguson, regarded as the university's founder.

**Shanghai Jiao Tong University** (**SJTU**; 上海交通大学, historically spelled **Shanghai Chiao Tung University**) is a public comprehensive university located in Shanghai, China. The university is affiliated with the Ministry of Education of China.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The university was established on April 8, 1896 as **Nanyang Public School** (南洋公學; *Nányáng Gōngxué*) by an imperial edict.[6][7] The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.[8] The university underwent a number of reformations and gained its current name in 1959. Shanghai Second Medical University was merged into the university on July 18, 2005.[9] It is a member of the C9 League.




## Name

[edit]

The word *Jiāotōng* (交通) (historically, **Chiao-t'ung**) means "transportation" or "communication". It reflects the university's roots — it was founded by the Ministry of Posts and Communications of the late Qing dynasty.[*citation needed*] Engineering and managerial sciences are major academic focuses at the various Jiaotong universities, but not the only fields of research.

<title>John Calvin Ferguson</title>
<fragment>

In 1889, Ferguson used the living room of his house in Nanjing for classes; these grew into Huiwen Shuyuan, which in turn evolved into the University of Nanking. In 1897 he was offered a position by Sheng Xuanhuai, a pioneering industrialist and well-connected entrepreneur whom he had met by chance a few years earlier when they were both on a Yangtze river boat. Sheng was impressed by Ferguson's learned Chinese and courtly manner and invited him to found a second western-style school, the Nanyang Public School, Shanghai, a predecessor of the Jiaotong (Transportation) University, which later split into three independent institutions: National Chiao Tung University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Xi'an Jiaotong University.[2] In 1897, to facilitate faculty and students getting to and from the school, he built a road in the Shanghai French Concession with his own salary,[3] which was later named Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road).[4]


</fragment>

When Ferguson resigned as president of the Nanyang school, with Sheng Xuanhuai's continuing sponsorship, he became foreign secretary to the Chinese Ministry of Commerce in 1903, and then was official or informal advisor to government bureaus and the chief secretary of the Imperial Chinese Railway Administration until 1907. Taking advantage of his knowledge and connections he began to acquire Chinese art for the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, Ferguson was a member of the committee to catalog the imperial palace collections of art.[1]

These volumes were unsystematic in the works they had access to and haphazard in their organization, but they made it possible to know the range and nature of Chinese art at a time when most of the important pieces were emerging from imperial or private collections which had not been available to the public or scholars.[2]


Ferguson donated many pieces to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, but the bulk of his own collection, including bronzes, scrolls, paintings, and jades, was donated to Nanjing University in 1935, and other major gifts were made which are now in the collections of Shanghai Jiao Tong University.[1]

<document>
<title>Higher education in China</title>
<fragment>
In 1895, Sheng Xuanhuai (Chinese: 盛宣懷) submitted a memorial to Guangxu Emperor to request for approval to set up a modern higher education institution in Tianjin. After approval on October 2, 1895, **Peiyang Western Study School** (Chinese: 天津北洋西學學堂) was founded by him and American educator Charles Daniel Tenney (Chinese: 丁家立) and later developed to **Peiyang University** (Chinese: 北洋大學堂). In 1896, Sheng Xuanhuai (Chinese: 盛宣懷) delivered his new memorials to Guangxu Emperor to make suggestion that two official modern higher education institutions should be established in Beijing and Shanghai. In the same year, he founded **Nanyang Public School** (Chinese: 南洋公學) in Shanghai by an imperial edict issued by Guangxu Emperor. The institution initially included elementary school, secondary school, college, and a normal school. Later the institution changed its name to **Jiao Tong University** (also known as **Chiao Tung University**, Chinese: 交通大學).

<fragment>
In 1921, the Ministry of Transport of Beiyang government founded Jiaotong University, with its headquarter in Beijing, and three branches in Beijing, Tangshan and Shanghai. The university was renamed Tangshan Institute of Jiaotong University. In 1922, the Ministry of Transport restructured Jiaotong University and divided it into Tangshan University and Nanyang University. The school was renamed as Tangshan University of the Ministry of Transport. In February 1928, Tangshan University was renamed Tangshan Jiaotong University under the instruction of Beiyang government. And in June, 1928, it was renamed the Second Jiaotong University after National Government's unifying South and South. In the same year, the Ministry of Transport restructured Jiaotong University and set its headquarter in Shanghai. The school was renamed Tangshan Civil Engineering Institute of Jiaotong University. In October, 1928, National Government founded Ministry of Railways, and the school was under its direct jurisdiction. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

Southwest Jiaotong University (SWJTU) was founded at Shanhaiguan in 1896, named then Imperial Chinese Railway College. It is one of the oldest universities in China majoring in engineering. In 1905, it was moved to Tangshan, Hebei Province, and was renamed Tangshan Chiao Tung University, Tangshan Railway Institute, and so on. In 1972, the university was removed to Emei, Sichuan province, and began to use its present name-Southwest Jiaotong University. In 1989, it was moved to Chengdu, and in 2002, the construction of a new campus covering an area of over 3,000 mu was started in Chengdu. With this, a new pattern of “one university, in two places, with three campuses” is coming into being.

Based on the Wikipedia research I've conducted, here's a comprehensive overview of Shanghai Jiao Tong University's founding and early history:

## Introduction

The history of Shanghai Jiao Tong University encompasses a complex evolution through multiple name changes and administrative reorganizations, reflecting China's turbulent transition from the late Qing dynasty through the Republican era. The institution exemplifies the Self-Strengthening Movement's approach to modernizing Chinese education through Western models.

## Founding During the Late Qing Dynasty (1896-1911)

**Nanyang Public School (南洋公学)** was founded in 1896 by imperial edict of the Guangxu Emperor, established under the Business and Telegraphs Office of the Qing imperial government. The founding emerged from the Self-Strengthening Movement's recognition that China needed modern technical education to build national strength.

### Co-Founders and Leadership

The institution was co-founded by **Sheng Xuanhuai**, a pioneering industrialist who served as Minister of Foreign Affairs, and **John Calvin Ferguson**, an American missionary and scholar. Ferguson, hired by Sheng in 1897 due to his learned Chinese and impressive background, served as the school's first president and even built a road (later named Route Ferguson, now Wukang Road) to facilitate access to the campus.

### Original Four-School Structure

Initially, the institution comprised four educational levels:
1. **Normal school** (师范院) - Teacher training
2. **School of foreign studies** (外院) - Language and international subjects  
3. **Middle school** (中院) - Secondary education
4. **High school** (上院) - Advanced/pre-collegiate education

### Educational Philosophy

Unlike some contemporary institutions that attempted to balance traditional Confucian education with Western learning, Nanyang Public School took a more practical approach focused on engineering, technology, railroad administration, and modern scientific education—reflecting Sheng Xuanhuai's industrial vision for modernizing China.

## Administrative Era and Name Changes

### Late Qing Period (1896-1911)
The school operated under Sheng Xuanhuai's sponsorship and was governed by the Ministry of Post and Transportation, reflecting its practical, industrial orientation rather than traditional educational administration.

### Early Republican Era (1912)

In 1912, following the Republic of China's establishment, the institution was renamed **Shanghai Industrial College** and came under the Ministry of Transportation. The vocational programs were expanded to include business, electrical engineering, shipping management, and railway management.

### Major Reorganization - Chiao Tung University Formation (1921)

In 1921, the Ministry of Transport (under the Beiyang government) created the unified **Chiao Tung University** system, bringing together three related institutions:
- **Shanghai campus** (the original Nanyang institution)
- **Tangshan campus** (originally Imperial Chinese Railway College, founded 1896, later Southwest Jiao Tang University)
- **Beijing campus**

This complex institutional history reveals how what became multiple modern Chinese universities originated from coordinated educational reforms during the Self-Strengthening Movement.

## Contemporary Legacy

The original Shanghai institution evolved into today's **Shanghai Jiao Tong University**, while the Tangshan branch became **Southwest Jiao Tong University** (now in Chengdu), and other branches led to institutions like **Xi'an Jiao Tong University** and **Beijing Jiao Tong University**.

## Significance in Chinese Educational History

Nanyang Public School represents a critical milestone in Chinese higher education modernization, demonstrating:
- The successful transplantation of Western technical education models
- The integration of educational reform with industrial development goals
- The entrepreneurial approach of late Qing reformers like Sheng Xuanhuai
- The professionalization of Chinese higher education beyond traditional Confucian models

The institution's evolution from a Qing dynasty public school to a leading modern research university mirrors China's broader modernization journey and the enduring influence of the Self-Strengthening Movement's educational reforms.

---
*Note: This analysis is based on available Wikipedia sources. For more detailed administrative records, curriculum specifics, and primary source documentation, researchers should consult university archives, specialized academic databases like CNKI, and comprehensive scholarly works on late Qing educational reforms.*

From 1929 to 1936 he served as director of the Chinese Institute of Meteorology of the Academia Sinica, which at the time was located in mainland China. The **Imperial Nanjing School**, the highest educational institution of kingdom, as the predecessor, was founded in CE 258 in the period of the Three Kingdoms. The imperial school enjoyed the same campus with the current Southeast University since the 14th year of Hongwu reign (CE 1381) in Ming dynasty.



### Sanjiang Normal College (三江师范学堂) (1902–1905)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Its precursor, Sanjiang Normal College, was established in 1902 as a modern university on the campus of an academy which dates back to 258. In 1921, the school changed its name to National Southeast University and became the second national university in China, and in 1928 was renamed to National Central University, the nation's flagship university.[4] After the Nationalist government lost Nanjing to the Chinese Communist Party during the Chinese Civil War, the university was renamed as National Nanking University in August 1949. It was renamed Southeast University in May 1988.

Based on my research from the available sources, I can provide you with a detailed analysis of Zhejiang University's early history and the conflicting founding dates. Here's what I've found:

## The Founding of Qiushi Academy in 1897

**Qiushi Academy (求是书院)** was founded in 1897 by **Lin Qi (林启)**, who was then the Mayor of Hangzhou. The academy was established on the site of a former temple (likely Pujǐ Temple) that had been damaged by fire six years earlier. 

**Lin Qi's motivations and purpose:**
- He was a reform-minded scholar-official who recognized the need for modern education in China
- The academy was focused on the so-called "New Learnings" or "New Subjects" (新学)
- It represented the shift away from traditional Confucian education toward modern Western-style education
- The name "Qiushi" (求是) means "seeking truth" or "pursuit of truth"

**Academic structure:**
- Five-year study duration
- Curriculum included Chinese, English, mathematics, history, geology/geography, physics, and chemistry
- Employed several foreign lecturers
- This was part of the broader education reforms happening in late Qing China

## The Evolution of Institutions (1897-1914)

The evolution proceeded as follows:

1. **Qiushi Academy (1897-1901)**
2. **Qiushi University (1901-1902)** - renamed to reflect university status
3. **Chekiang University (1902-1903)** - part of the 1902 education reforms
4. **Chekiang Higher Institutes (1903-1914)** - further reorganization
5. **Closure (1914-1927)**

## What Happened During the Closure Period (1914-1927)

The sources indicate significant disruption during this period, likely related to:
- Political instability in early Republican China
- Educational reforms and reorganizations
- Warlordism and political instability
- The centralized vs. decentralized nature of education during this time

## The 1902 vs. 1927 Founding Date Conflict

### Why 1902 is cited:
- **1902 was a pivotal year for Chinese higher education reform** - The Qing government issued "The imperial rules for colleges" and adapted a modern education system
- Many Chinese universities trace their modern institutional existence to **1902 reforms**
- Similar to how other universities (like Southeast University's Sanjiang Normal College) were established in 1902 as part of these nationwide reforms
- This represents the **establishment of the modern university structure**

### Why 1927 is cited:
- **National Third Chungsan University (1927-1928)** was founded as a completely new institution
- This was part of the Nationalist government's educational reorganization
- The closure from 1914-1927 represents a **break in institutional continuity**
- Some argue this represents the **true founding of the continuous institutional line**

## Key Founders and Motivations

**Lin Qi (林启)** was the crucial early figure:
- Mayor of Hangzhou when Qiushi Academy was founded
- Vision of blending traditional Chinese education with modern Western approaches
- Part of the reform movement that sought to modernize Chinese education

**Later leadership:**
- **Chu Coching (竺可桢)** (1936-1949) was pivotal in elevating National Chekiang University to prestige
- His famous quote about university education: "The aim of university education is not to nurture experts such as engineers and doctors, but to build leaders that are just, patriotic, fortitudinous and persistent..."

## Institutional Continuity Analysis

The question of continuity is complex:

**Arguments for continuity (earlier founding):**
- Same geographical location in Hangzhou
- Educational mission continuation
- Faculty and student transitions
- Lin Qi's foundational role

**Arguments against continuity (later founding):**
- **13-year gap from 1914-1927** represents a true break
- Different institutional structures and governance
- Different political contexts (Qing vs. Republican era)
- National Third Chungsan University was established as a completely new entity

## The Broader Context

This mirrors patterns across Chinese higher education:
- Many universities have similar founding date disputations
- The 1902 reforms were transformative across China
- Early Republic period (1911-1927) was chaotic for educational institutions
- Nationalist reorganization in 1927 created many new "National" universities

## Conclusion

The conflicting founding dates reflect **different interpretations of institutional identity**:
- **1897** recognizes Lin Qi's pioneering educational vision and the earliest roots
- **1902** emphasizes the modern university structure and nationwide educational reforms
- **1927** focuses on continuous institutional existence from the Nationalist era

Most comprehensive sources acknowledge this complexity, listing the full evolution chain while noting the closure period as a significant interruption. The "correct" founding date depends on whether one prioritizes **educational mission continuity** (favoring earlier dates) or **formal institutional continuity** (favoring 1927).

For your research, you should emphasize that **Zhejiang University claims multiple founding dates for different aspects of its heritage**, with 1897 representing the spirit of innovation, 1902 representing modern university structure, and 1927 representing continuous institutional existence.

7. **National Chekiang University** (1928-1950) - Established by Nationalist government
8. **Chekiang University** (1950-1958) - Post-revolution name
9. **Zhejiang University** (1958-present) - Current name

## **Critical Historical Context**

### **The 13-Year Gap (1914-1927)**
The closure was caused by:
- Political instability of early Republican China
- Warlordism and decentralization
- Educational funding and administrative disruptions
- National education system chaos following the 1911 Revolution

### **1927 Reestablishment**
- **Founded as:** A completely new institution by the Nationalist government
- **Starting size:** 174 students
- **Context:** Part of systematic educational reorganization after the Northern Expedition

## **Academic Consensus**

Most comprehensive historical sources acknowledge:
- **1897** represents the earliest educational roots and institutional spirit
- **1902** represents the establishment of modern university structure  
- **1927** represents continuous institutional existence

The appropriate founding date depends on whether one prioritizes **educational mission continuity** (favoring 1897/1902) or **formal institutional continuity** (favoring 1927).

Zhejiang University itself acknowledges this complex heritage by:
- Maintaining "Qiushi" (seeking truth) in its motto
- Using the "Qiushi Eagle" as its mascot
- Recognizing Lin Qi's 1897 vision as foundational to its educational spirit

This pattern of founding date complexity is common among Chinese universities due to the dramatic political and educational transformations of the late Qing and early Republican periods.

## **各大学成立时间和关键信息**

### **1. 北京大学**
- **成立时间：** 1898年7月3日
- **成立背景：** 戊戌变法期间，光绪帝敕令建立
- **创始人：** 光绪帝、康有为、梁启超、严复倡导，李鸿章具体实施
- **原名：** 京师大学堂（Imperial University of Peking）
- **早期更名：** 1912年→国立北京大学，1919年→国立北京大学

### **2. 复旦大学**
- **成立时间：** 1905年
- **创始人：** 马相伯（耶稣会士）
- **原名：** 复旦公学
- **成立背景：** 马相伯离开震旦大学后创办，"复旦"意为"日月光华，旦复旦兮"
- **早期更名：** 1917年→私立复旦大学，1941年→国立复旦大学

### **3. 南京大学**
- **成立时间：** 1902年（现代大学形式）
- **创始人：** 张之洞、刘坤一、韦光涛
- **原名：** 三江师范学堂
- **历史传承：** 可追溯至258年三国时期的太学
- **早期更名：** 1911年→两江师范学堂，1915年→南京高等师范学校，后→国立东南大学→国立中央大学

### **4. 上海交通大学**
- **成立时间：** 1896年4月8日
- **创始人：** 盛宣怀（主要创始人）、John Calvin Ferguson（首任校长）
- **原名：** 南洋公学
- **成立背景：** 洋务运动期间，专注工程技术和铁路管理教育
- **早期更名：** 1912年→上海工业专门学校，后→交通大学

### **5. 浙江大学**
- **成立时间：** 1897年（教育根源）→ 1927年（连续机构存在）
- **创始人：** 林启（时任杭州知府）
- **原名：** 求是书院
- **特殊历史：** 1914-1927年间曾停办13年，1927年重新建立
- **早期更名：** 1901年→求是大学堂，后多次更名，1958年→浙江大学

## **时间顺序总结**
1. **上海交通大学**（1896年）- 最早成立
2. **北京大学**（1898年）- 第二早
3. **浙江大学**（1897年教育根源）
4. **复旦大学**（1905年）
5. **南京大学**（1902年现代大学形式）

## **共同特点**
- 都诞生于晚清教育改革时期
- 深受西方教育模式影响
- 经历了复杂的名称更替和重组过程
- 见证了中国近代教育的现代化历程
- 多数与洋务运动、维新变法等历史运动密切相关

这五所大学每所都有独特的历史背景和发展轨迹，反映了中国近现代教育发展的不同路径和特色。

<title>Fudan University</title>
<fragment>

Fudan is a member of the C9 League, Project 985, Project 211, and the Double First Class University identified by the Ministry of Education of China. It is also a member of Universitas 21, Washington University's McDonnell International Scholars Academy, and the Association of Pacific Rim Universities, BRICS Universities League, Association of East Asian Research Universities, and Council on Business & Society.


Fudan University is a member of the Consortium of Academic Stewards for The Scholar Ship. The university is also a member of China Center Austria and partner of the Austrian Business School SMBS.


In February 2008, Fudan University launched the Fudan University Education Development Foundation in New York. [40]


In 1995, Fudan established the Nordic Centre in Shanghai, a joint platform for research and education with 14 universities from Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden. By 2012, the Nordic Centre Fudan has 27 member institutions in 5 Nordic countries.[41]


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Fudan lost its "National" appellation and became Fudan University to reflect the fact that all universities under the new socialist state would be public. Fudan was the first university to be reorganized by the new government in 1952 and modeled on Soviet education. The original departments were changed, with arts and sciences departments from at least ten other universities in eastern China being added.[*citation needed*] Parts of Aurora University merged into Fudan in 1952.


In the late 1970s, after the Cultural Revolution, the university was converted to a modern, comprehensive[*clarification needed*] university.[*citation needed*]


Fudan University and Shanghai Medical University merged in 2000.[5]

**Fudan University** (复旦大学) is a national public university in Shanghai, China. The university is affiliated with the Ministry of Education, and is co-sponsored by the ministry and Shanghai City. The university is part of Project 985, Project 211, and the Double First Class University Plan.


Fudan has five undergraduate colleges – Zhide (志德), Tengfei (腾飞), Keqing (克卿), Renzhong (任重), and Xide (希德). The university has four campuses in Shanghai – Handan (邯郸), Fenglin (枫林), Zhangjiang (张江), and Jiangwan (江湾) – which share the same central administration. It also has 17 affiliated hospitals. The university is a member of the C9 League.

The university survived with altered objectives and reduced scope. It opened on 31 December with 160 students, instead of the planned 500.[7]


In 1900, the university was paralyzed by the Boxer Rebellion, later in the year, the "Eight-Power Allied Forces" (八国联军) entered Beijing and the university's operation was continually suspended. In 1902, "Jingshi Tongwenguan", a school established by the Qing court in 1862 for foreign language learning was incorporated into the Imperial University of Peking. In 1904, the university sent 47 students to study abroad, which marked the first time for Chinese higher education institution to send students to foreign countries.


Following the Xinhai Revolution, the Imperial University of Peking was renamed "Government University of Peking" in 1912 and then "National University of Peking" in 1919[8] (simplified Chinese: 国立北京大学; traditional Chinese: 國立北京大學; pinyin: *Guólì Běijīng Dàxué*).

**Nanjing University** (**NJU**; Chinese: 南京大学) is a national public university in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. It is affiliated and sponsored by the Ministry of Education. The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.


Established in 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School, Nanjing University underwent a number of name changes, such as Nanjing Higher Normal School, National Southeastern University and National Central University, until it was renamed Nanjing University in 1950. It merged with the University of Nanking in 1952.[6]


Nanjing University has two main campuses: the Xianlin campus in the northeast of Nanjing, and the Gulou campus in the city center of Nanjing. The university is a member of the C9 League.

<document>
<title>Peking University</title>
<fragment>
Following China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War, intellectuals - including Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao, and Yan Fu - called for reforms to the country's education system. In June 1896, Minister Li Duanfen proposed to create a university in the capital. On 11 June 1898, the Guangxu Emperor, as part of the Hundred Days' Reform, authorised the creation of the **Imperial University of Peking**[7] (simplified Chinese: 京师大学堂; traditional Chinese: 京師大學堂; pinyin: *Jīngshī Dàxuétáng*; lit. 'Capital Grand Study Hall').[8] The Imperial University was formally established on 3 July 1898 when the emperor approved the royal charter written by Liang. Minister Sun Jianai was charged with the implementation. IUP served as the country's foremost institute for higher learning, but also as its highest educational authority.[7] William Alexander Parsons Martin was appointed as the first president.[8] Most of the reforms were abolished when the conservative Empress Dowager Cixi seized power on 21 September. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
The university survived with altered objectives and reduced scope. It opened on 31 December with 160 students, instead of the planned 500.[7]


In 1900, the university was paralyzed by the Boxer Rebellion, later in the year, the "Eight-Power Allied Forces" (八国联军) entered Beijing and the university's operation was continually suspended. In 1902, "Jingshi Tongwenguan", a school established by the Qing court in 1862 for foreign language learning was incorporated into the Imperial University of Peking. In 1904, the university sent 47 students to study abroad, which marked the first time for Chinese higher education institution to send students to foreign countries.


Following the Xinhai Revolution, the Imperial University of Peking was renamed "Government University of Peking" in 1912 and then "National University of Peking" in 1919[8] (simplified Chinese: 国立北京大学; traditional Chinese: 國立北京大學; pinyin: *Guólì Běijīng Dàxué*).

<document>
<title>Cai Yuanpei</title>
<fragment>

**Cai Yuanpei** (Chinese: 蔡元培; pinyin: *Cài Yuánpéi*; 1868–1940) was a Chinese philosopher and politician who was an influential figure in the history of Chinese modern education. He made contributions to education reform with his own education ideology. He was the president of Peking University, and founder of the Academia Sinica. He was known for his critical evaluation of Chinese culture and synthesis of Chinese and Western thinking, including anarchism. He got involved in the New Culture, May Fourth Movements, and the feminist movement. His works involve aesthetic education, politics, education reform, etc.




## Biography

[edit]

![](image)Cai's former residence in Shaoxing, Zhejiang.
Born in Shanyin County, Shaoxing prefecture, Zhejiang, Cai was appointed to the Hanlin Imperial Academy at 26. In 1898, he became involved in administering institutes and became:




</fragment>

* Wang Peili (1996). *Wilhelm von Humboldt und Cai Yuanpei: eine vergleichende Analyse zweier klassischer Bildungskonzepte in der deutschen Aufklärung und in der ersten chinesischen Republik* (in German). Münster, New York: Waxmann.
* Boorman, Howard L. (1970). "T'sai Yuan-p'ei". *Biographical Dictionary of Republican China Vol III*. New York: Columbia University Press. pp. 295=299. ISBN 0231045581.
* Timothy B. Weston. *The Power of Position: Beijing University, Intellectuals, and Chinese Political Culture, 1898-1929.* (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2004; ISBN 0520237676).

International Journal of Psychology, 36(6), 2001, 408. doi:10.1080/00207590143000234

"Politics and Education in Nationalist China: The Case of the University Council, 1927-1928". *The Journal of Asian Studies*. **27** (4): 763–776. doi:10.2307/2051578. ISSN 0021-9118. JSTOR 2051578. S2CID 154280190. Archived from the original on 2020-10-09. Retrieved 2020-10-08.

</fragment>
<fragment>
Cai Yuanpei raised the traditional virtue of “righteousness (义), reciprocity (恕) and humanity (仁)” based on the Western ideas of "Freedom, equity, fraternity".[3] He was committed to establishing academic freedom and a pure research atmosphere at Peking University. He also tried to protect the freedom of educators and students, in education reform.[3] Among the teaching staff at Peking University, there were many representatives of the new cultural movement such as Li Dazhao, Hu Shih, and Chen Duxiu. He also assembled notable conservative and old-fashioned scholars such as Gu Hongming and Liu Shipei to teaching at Peking University.[9]



### Five types of education

[edit]

He advocated practising five types of education in the education system. The five types of education refer to military education for citizen (军国民教育), utilitarian education (实利主义教育), civic education (公民道德教育), education for a world view (世界观教育), and aesthetic education (美感学教育)."[3]

In 1976, Nanjing University faculty members and students launched Anti Cultural Revolution Force Movement which was called "Nanjing Incident" by the authorities of the time, spreading countrywide. In 1978, Hu Fuming, a faculty member of Nanjing University in philosophy, wrote the historic article entitled "Practice is the Sole Criterion for Testing Truth", and after being published it led to the nationwide "Debate on Standards for Judging the Truth", and thus in certain degree liberated thought and promoted the ending of Cultural Revolution and the coming of reform era.

Based on my research, I can provide you with comparisons of the founding intentions and educational philosophies of several key Chinese universities. Here are the detailed comparisons:

## 1. Peking University (北京大学) - 1916 Reform under Cai Yuanpei

**Background:** Founded in 1898 as Imperial University of Peking, but truly transformed under President Cai Yuanpei in 1916.

**Cai Yuanpei's Educational Philosophy:**
- **Academic Freedom:** Cai was committed to establishing complete academic freedom and a pure research atmosphere at Peking University.
- **Ideological Diversity:** He brought together both progressive thinkers (like Chen Duxiu, Hu Shih, Li Dazhao) and conservative scholars (like Gu Hongming, Liu Shipei), creating an environment of intellectual pluralism.
- **Synthesis of East and West:** Cai aimed to synthesize traditional Chinese virtues with Western ideas, basing traditional values of "righteousness (义), reciprocity (恕) and humanity (仁)" on Western concepts of "Freedom, equity, fraternity."
- **Five Types of Education:** He advocated for a comprehensive educational system including: military education for citizens, utilitarian education, civic moral education, worldview education, and aesthetic education.

**Key Differences from Others:** Unlike vocational or technical institutions, Peking University under Cai emphasized pure academic research, intellectual exploration, and cultural transformation rather than practical skills training.

## 2. Nanjing University (南京大学) - Sanjiang Normal School (1902)

**Background:** Established in 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School, evolving through several name changes including Liangjiang Normal College.

**Educational Philosophy:**
- **Normal School Tradition:** Originally founded as a teacher training institution, following Japanese modern higher education models.
- **Westernized Modern Education:** Used Japanese institutions as templates for modernizing Chinese education while replacing traditional Chinese schools like Nanking Academy.
- **Practical Application:** President Li Ruiqing established China's first faculty of modern art, showing emphasis on practical, applied education.
- **Scientific Focus:** The university developed strong scientific traditions, producing leading scientists who contributed significantly to China's modernization.

**Key Differences:** Unlike Peking University's focus on academic freedom and intellectual debate, Nanjing University maintained stronger emphasis on practical training, particularly in teacher education and applied sciences.

## 3. Shanghai Jiao Tong University (交通大学) - Nanyang Public School (1896)

**Background:** Founded in 1896 as Nanyang Public School by imperial edict under the Guangxu Emperor, proposed by Sheng Xuanhuai.

**Educational Philosophy:**
- **Self-Strengthening Movement:** Rooted in the late Qing Self-Strengthening Movement, emphasizing using Western technology to strengthen China.
- **Practical Technical Education:** Initially established four schools: normal school, foreign studies, middle school, and high school, with strong emphasis on practical skills.
- **Engineering and Technology Focus:** Sheng Xuanhuai was involved in railways, telegraphy, ironworks, and saw education as essential for China's industrial development.
- **Western Technology Transfer:** The institution was explicitly designed to import and adapt Western technical knowledge for China's modernization.

**Key Differences:** Much more vocational and technically oriented than Peking University, focusing on engineering, technology, and practical applications rather than pure academic research or liberal arts.

## 4. University of Science and Technology of China (中国科学技术大学) - 1958

**Background:** Founded in Beijing by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 1958, moved to Hefei in 1970 during the Cultural Revolution.

**Educational Philosophy:**
- **Science-Integration Model:** Created to integrate research with education, bringing together the Chinese Academy of Sciences' research capabilities with university education.
- **Cutting-Edge Science Focus:** Emphasized advanced scientific research and education, particularly in emerging fields.
- **State-led Development:** Founded to support China's scientific and technological development goals during the early People's Republic period.
- **Research-University Model:** Combined teaching with advanced scientific research, with many national research platforms integrated into the university structure.

**Key Differences:** Much more research-intensive and state-directed than the earlier institutions, specifically designed to advance China's scientific capabilities rather than broader educational reform.

## Comparative Summary:

**Educational Approaches:**
- **Peking University:** Liberal arts, academic freedom, intellectual pluralism
- **Nanjing University:** Teacher training, applied sciences, Westernized modern education
- **Shanghai Jiao Tong:** Technical and engineering education, practical skills, industrial development
- **USTC:** Research-intensive, cutting-edge science, state-directed development

**Historical Contexts:**
- **Peking University (1916):** Post-imperial intellectual awakening, New Culture Movement
- **Nanjing University (1902):** Late Qing educational reform, Japanese influence
- **Shanghai Jiao Tong (1896):** Self-Strengthening Movement, industrial modernization
- **USTC (1958):** Socialist construction, scientific advancement

Each institution reflected China's contemporary needs and historical context, from Peking University's role in cultural and intellectual transformation to USTC's focus on scientific excellence for national development.

The university survived with altered objectives and reduced scope. It opened on 31 December with 160 students, instead of the planned 500.[7]


In 1900, the university was paralyzed by the Boxer Rebellion, later in the year, the "Eight-Power Allied Forces" (八国联军) entered Beijing and the university's operation was continually suspended. In 1902, "Jingshi Tongwenguan", a school established by the Qing court in 1862 for foreign language learning was incorporated into the Imperial University of Peking. In 1904, the university sent 47 students to study abroad, which marked the first time for Chinese higher education institution to send students to foreign countries.


Following the Xinhai Revolution, the Imperial University of Peking was renamed "Government University of Peking" in 1912 and then "National University of Peking" in 1919[8] (simplified Chinese: 国立北京大学; traditional Chinese: 國立北京大學; pinyin: *Guólì Běijīng Dàxué*).

<fragment>

Cai returned to China in 1916 and served as the President of Peking University the following year. There he resumed his support, begun in his Paris years with Li Shizeng, for the Diligent Work-Frugal Study Movement, which sent worker-students to France.[3] It was during his tenure at Peking University that he recruited such famous thinkers (and future Chinese Communist Party leaders) to the school as Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, as well as quite different thinkers as Hu Shih, a close friend, Liang Shuming and the painter Xu Beihong.[4]

<fragment>

**Cai Yuanpei** (Chinese: 蔡元培; pinyin: *Cài Yuánpéi*; 1868–1940) was a Chinese philosopher and politician who was an influential figure in the history of Chinese modern education. He made contributions to education reform with his own education ideology. He was the president of Peking University, and founder of the Academia Sinica. He was known for his critical evaluation of Chinese culture and synthesis of Chinese and Western thinking, including anarchism. He got involved in the New Culture, May Fourth Movements, and the feminist movement. His works involve aesthetic education, politics, education reform, etc.

**Nanjing University** (**NJU**; Chinese: 南京大学) is a national public university in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. It is affiliated and sponsored by the Ministry of Education. The university is part of the Double First Class University Plan, Project 985, and Project 211.


Established in 1902 as Sanjiang Normal School, Nanjing University underwent a number of name changes, such as Nanjing Higher Normal School, National Southeastern University and National Central University, until it was renamed Nanjing University in 1950. It merged with the University of Nanking in 1952.[6]


Nanjing University has two main campuses: the Xianlin campus in the northeast of Nanjing, and the Gulou campus in the city center of Nanjing. The university is a member of the C9 League.

Originally as **Imperial Tientsin University** and later **Peiyang University**, the university was founded with the goal of providing modern education in engineering and mining, and it later expanded to include programs in science, business, law, humanities, and other fields. The establishment of Tianjin University marked a turning point in Chinese history, as it represented a significant shift towards modernization and the adoption of Western educational models.[3]
